props.title: The City of Violence

sections.content: The City of Violence represents a pivotal moment in South Korean action cinema, building on the momentum of films like Oldboy (2003) and A Bittersweet Life (2005). Director Ryoo Seung-wan crafts a hyperkinetic revenge thriller that pays homage to classic martial arts films while incorporating modern urban violence. The film's influence can be seen in later works like The Man from Nowhere (2010) and The Villainess (2017), establishing a distinctly Korean approach to action choreography that emphasizes raw intensity over wire-work spectacle.

sections.content: The fight choreography in The City of Violence draws clear inspiration from Hong Kong cinema classics like Police Story (1985) and Hard Boiled (1992), but adds distinctly Korean elements - particularly in its use of traditional weapons and street fighting techniques. The film's legendary five-on-one alley fight scene demonstrates Ryoo's ability to balance classical martial arts with modern urban combat, influencing later works like The Night Comes for Us (2018) and The Raid: Redemption (2011).

Beyond its action sequences, The City of Violence explores themes common to Korean crime cinema - loyalty, betrayal, and the corruption of childhood friendship. These themes echo through films like Friend (2001) and New World (2013), creating a distinctive subset of Korean action-noir that combines emotional depth with explosive violence. sections.content: The success of The City of Violence helped pave the way for a new wave of Korean action films that emphasized practical stunts and realistic combat over CGI. Films like The Yellow Sea (2010) and I Saw the Devil (2010) followed this template, combining intense action with dark storytelling. This approach culminated in works like The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil (2019), which continued the tradition of grounding fantastic action sequences in emotionally resonant narratives.
